conceptPrimer.heading: Matrix Anatomy: Order, Entries & Equality
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A matrix $A = [a_{ij}]_{m \times n}$ is a rectangular array with $m$ rows and $n$ columns; the entry $a_{ij}$ sits in row $i$, column $j$, and an $m \times n$ matrix holds $mn$ elements — so a matrix with 18 elements can only be $1\times18, 18\times1, 2\times9, 9\times2, 3\times6$ or $6\times3$. Addition and scalar multiplication act entry-by-entry, but multiplication is the star rule: $AB$ exists only when the inner orders agree (columns of $A$ = rows of $B$), the result is $m \times q$, and entry $(i,j)$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of $B$. Multiplication is associative and distributive, but NOT commutative: micro-check — for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $AB = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ while $BA = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. Equality of matrices means equal order AND every entry equal — one matrix equation therefore hides a whole system of scalar equations, which is exactly how JELET hides unknowns inside $A = B$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Transpose & the Symmetry Split
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: The transpose $A^T$ flips a matrix across its main diagonal (row $i$ becomes column $i$). Its laws are short and examinable: $(A^T)^T = A$, $(A+B)^T = A^T + B^T$, $(kA)^T = kA^T$, and the reversal law $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$ — transpose reverses order, like removing shoes before socks. Any square matrix splits uniquely as $A = \frac{1}{2}(A + A^T) + \frac{1}{2}(A - A^T)$: the plus part is symmetric ($S^T = S$), the minus part is skew-symmetric ($K^T = -K$, with every diagonal entry $0$). Two consequences JELET loves: if $A$ and $B$ are both symmetric then $AB$ need not be symmetric (that needs $AB = BA$), but the commutator $AB - BA$ is ALWAYS skew-symmetric, since $(AB - BA)^T = B^TA^T - A^TB^T = -(AB - BA)$. Micro-check: $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ — symmetric plus skew, rebuilt exactly.

conceptPrimer.heading: Determinant Essentials Every Matrix Question Uses
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A determinant turns a square matrix into one number; only square matrices have one. The order-2 value is $ad - bc$; order-3 expands along any row or column as $\sum_j (-1)^{i+j} a_{ij} M_{ij}$. Four properties do most exam work: $|kA| = k^n|A|$ (the order comes out FIRST — for $3\times3$, $|2A| = 8|A|$); $|AB| = |A||B|$ and $|A^T| = |A|$; swapping two rows flips the sign, two identical rows force $|A| = 0$; and a triangular (or diagonal) matrix has determinant equal to the product of its diagonal entries. One masterpiece shortcut: for skew-symmetric $A$, $|A^T| = |-A| = (-1)^n |A|$, so an odd-order skew-symmetric matrix forces $|A| = -|A|$, hence $|A| = 0$ — quote it, never expand it. Micro-check: $|2 \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}| = 2^2 \cdot (4 - 6) = -8$. Full determinant machinery (minors, Cramer, area) belongs to Unit M02; here we use only the laws matrices need.

conceptPrimer.heading: The Adjoint-Inverse Engine
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Cofactors first, flip last: build $C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$, transpose the cofactor matrix, and you hold $\operatorname{adj}A$. The engine driving every adjoint question is $A \cdot \operatorname{adj}A = \operatorname{adj}A \cdot A = |A| I_n$, and it pays out three ways: divide by $|A|$ to get $A^{-1} = \frac{\operatorname{adj}A}{|A|}$ (only when $|A| \neq 0$ — a singular matrix has no inverse, stop there); take determinants to get $|\operatorname{adj}A| = |A|^{n-1}$; substitute $A \to \operatorname{adj}A$ to get $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A) = |A|^{n-2}A$. For order 2 skip cofactors entirely: $\operatorname{adj}\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$ — swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal. Micro-check: if $|A| = 5$ for order 3, then $|\operatorname{adj}A| = 5^2 = 25$ and $|A \cdot \operatorname{adj}A| = |A|^3 = 125$ — ten seconds, zero expansion.

conceptPrimer.heading: Special Squares and Their One-Line Tests
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Special matrices are identified by one equation, and that equation answers everything. Orthogonal: $AA^T = A^T A = I$ — rows (and columns) are orthonormal, $A^{-1} = A^T$, and $|A|^2 = 1$ forces $|A| = \pm 1$. Involutory: $A^2 = I$ — the matrix is its own inverse. Idempotent: $A^2 = A$ — taking determinants gives $|A|^2 = |A|$, so $|A| = 0$ or $1$. Nilpotent: $A^k = O$ for some $k$ — determinants force $|A| = 0$, so nilpotent matrices are always singular. Powers also follow one line: $(kI_n)^p = k^p I_n$, and diagonal matrices are raised to powers entry-by-entry. Micro-check: $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ is simultaneously orthogonal and involutory ($A^2 = I$, $A^{-1} = A = A^T$, $|A| = -1$) — one tiny matrix demonstrating two tests at once.

conceptPrimer.heading: Cayley-Hamilton & Trace: The Power Crusher
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation $|\lambda I - A| = 0$ — replace $\lambda$ by $A$ and any high power collapses into $A$ and $I$. For order 2 the polynomial is $\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda + |A| = 0$, so $A^2 = (\operatorname{tr}A)A - |A|I$; for order 3 it is $\lambda^3 - (\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda^2 + (\text{sum of principal 2nd-order minors})\lambda - |A| = 0$. Multiplying the relation by $A^{-1}$ even manufactures the inverse: micro-check — if $\operatorname{tr}A = 3$ and $|A| = 2$, then $A^2 = 3A - 2I$, and dividing by $A$ gives $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}(3I - A)$. The trace is the free sidekick: $\operatorname{tr}(kA) = k\,\operatorname{tr}A$, $\operatorname{tr}(A+B) = \operatorname{tr}A + \operatorname{tr}B$, and the cyclic law $\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$ — true even when $AB \neq BA$ — is a one-mark gift. Use the trace or determinant of your final matrix as a self-check whenever time allows.

keyFormulas.label: Transpose Laws & Reversal
keyFormulas.latex: $(A^T)^T = A,\; (A \pm B)^T = A^T \pm B^T,\; (AB)^T = B^T A^T$
keyFormulas.use: Reverse the order whenever a product is transposed.

keyFormulas.label: Unique Symmetric + Skew Split
keyFormulas.use: Decompose any square matrix; identify each part on sight.

keyFormulas.label: Commutator Skew Theorem
keyFormulas.use: Difference of products of symmetric matrices is always skew-symmetric.

keyFormulas.label: Scalar-Multiple Determinant
keyFormulas.use: Apply the order $n$ before the value of $k$ (order 3, $k=2$: factor 8).

keyFormulas.label: Product & Transpose Determinants
keyFormulas.use: Split products; transpose never changes the determinant.

keyFormulas.label: Inverse Determinant
keyFormulas.use: Determinant of an inverse is the reciprocal (non-singular only).

keyFormulas.label: Odd-Order Skew Determinant
keyFormulas.use: Quote directly — never expand the determinant.

keyFormulas.label: Triangular/Diagonal Determinant
keyFormulas.use: Read the answer off the diagonal — zero expansion time.

keyFormulas.label: Adjoint Identity
keyFormulas.use: The engine of every adjoint question; also verifies your adjoint arithmetic.

keyFormulas.label: Inverse via Adjoint
keyFormulas.use: Compute $|A|$ first; singular means stop — no inverse exists.

keyFormulas.label: Order-2 Adjoint Shortcut
keyFormulas.latex: $\operatorname{adj}\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$
keyFormulas.use: Swap diagonal, negate off-diagonal — skip cofactors entirely.

keyFormulas.label: Orthogonal Matrix Test
keyFormulas.use: One equation certifies orthogonality and pins the determinant.

keyFormulas.label: Cayley-Hamilton Characteristic Equations
keyFormulas.use: Substitute $A$ to crush high powers; divide by $A$ to express $A^{-1}$.

keyFormulas.label: Trace Laws (Cyclic Product)
keyFormulas.use: Cyclic trace holds even when $AB \neq BA$ — free one-mark checks.

keyDefinitions.definition: An ordered rectangular array $[a_{ij}]$ of $m$ rows and $n$ columns; $m \times n$ is its order and $mn$ is its element count.
Square matrix with off-diagonal entries zero (diagonal); a diagonal matrix with equal diagonal entries $k$ (scalar); the scalar matrix with $k = 1$, denoted $I_n$ (identity).
A square matrix with $A^T = A$, equivalently $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i, j$.
A square matrix with $A^T = -A$, equivalently $a_{ij} = -a_{ji}$; every diagonal entry is $0$.
A square matrix is singular when $|A| = 0$ (no inverse) and non-singular when $|A| \neq 0$ (inverse exists).
The minor $M_{ij}$ is the determinant left after deleting row $i$ and column $j$; the cofactor is $C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$.
The transpose of the cofactor matrix of a square matrix; it satisfies $A\,\operatorname{adj}A = |A|I_n$ whether or not $A$ is invertible.
A real square matrix with $AA^T = A^T A = I$; equivalently its rows (and columns) form an orthonormal set and $|A| = \pm 1$.
The sum of the diagonal entries of a square matrix; cyclic under products: $\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$.
Matrix power families: idempotent $A^2 = A$; involutory $A^2 = I$ (self-inverse); nilpotent $A^k = O$ for some $k$ (always singular).

mcqSelfTest.explanation: $|kA| = k^n|A|$ with $n = 3$: $|2A| = 2^3 \cdot 3 = 8 \times 3 = 24$. The order is applied before the scalar.

mcqSelfTest.explanation: $|A^T| = |-A| = (-1)^n|A| = -|A|$ for odd $n$, so $|A| = -|A|$ forces $|A| = 0$. (Even-order skew determinants are perfect squares, not this case.)
Order-2 shortcut: swap the diagonal ($3 \leftrightarrow 4$), negate the off-diagonal ($1 \to -1$, $2 \to -2$). No cofactor expansion needed.

memoryHooks: Transpose reverses order: $(AB)^T = B^TA^T$ — undo in reverse, like shoes before socks.
Adjoint recipe: cofactors first, flip (transpose) last.
$A^{-1} = \operatorname{adj}A/|A|$ — no determinant, no inverse: $|A| = 0$ means stop.
Order-2 adjoint = swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal.
Odd-order skew-symmetric: determinant is $0$ — quote it, never expand.
Orthogonal test $AA^T = I$ pins $|A| = \pm 1$ and hands you $A^{-1} = A^T$.
Cayley-Hamilton kills powers: write the characteristic polynomial, substitute $A$.
Symmetric split uses plus, skew split uses minus: $\tfrac{1}{2}(A \pm A^T)$.
Trace is cyclic: $\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$ even when $AB \neq BA$.
commonMistakes: Multiplying in the wrong order: $AB$ walks rows of the LEFT matrix into columns of the RIGHT one — swapping operands silently changes every entry, and $AB \neq BA$ in general.
Building the cofactor matrix but forgetting the final transpose while forming $\operatorname{adj}A$.
Attempting $\operatorname{adj}A$ or $A^{-1}$ for a rectangular matrix — only square matrices carry an adjoint and an inverse.
Dropping the alternating sign $(-1)^{i+j}$ while computing cofactors — one flipped sign ruins both $\operatorname{adj}A$ and $|A|$.
Collapsing $(A+B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2$ into $A^2 + 2AB + B^2$ — that needs $AB = BA$, which is not given.
Applying $|kA| = k|A|$ without raising to the order $n$ first.
Hunting for an inverse when $|A| = 0$ — the question is usually testing exactly this realisation.
Reading $|A|$ as the entrywise absolute value of $A$ — the bars denote a determinant (one number), not per-entry magnitude.
Mixing power laws of scalars and matrices: $(kA)^p = k^p A^p$ and $(kI_n)^p = k^p I_n$, not $kA^p$.
examChecklist: Write the order of every matrix before multiplying — inner orders must agree, outer orders give the result.
Decompose on sight: $\tfrac{1}{2}(A + A^T)$ is symmetric, $\tfrac{1}{2}(A - A^T)$ is skew-symmetric.
Scalar-multiple determinant: raise the scalar to the order $n$ before plugging values.
Odd-order skew-symmetric: quote $|A| = 0$ without any expansion.
Inverse pipeline: $|A|$ → cofactors → transpose → divide; bail out politely if $|A| = 0$.
Self-check an adjoint with $A \cdot \operatorname{adj}A = |A|I$ on one diagonal entry.
For $2 \times 2$, use the swap-negate shortcut instead of cofactor expansion.
Cayley-Hamilton: write the characteristic polynomial first, substitute $A$, isolate the power or $A^{-1}$ needed.
Run the special-matrix tests in order: $AA^T = I$? $A^2 = I$? $A^2 = A$? $A^k = O$?
Use trace laws for one-line answers: $\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$, $\operatorname{tr}(A + B) = \operatorname{tr}A + \operatorname{tr}B$.
Sanity-check the final determinant of any product: $|AB| = |A||B|$ — if your value breaks this, recompute.
